questions.question: Why was Raft created as an alternative to Paxos?

options.text: Paxos was too slow for modern distributed systems
To provide an understandable consensus algorithm that's easier to implement correctly
Paxos was patented and required licensing fees
Raft uses significantly less memory than Paxos

questions.explanation: Raft was designed explicitly for understandability. Paxos is notoriously hard to understand—Leslie Lamport's original paper was rejected for being 'too Greek.' Raft decomposes consensus into leader election, log replication, and safety—each easier to reason about. The Raft paper won a USENIX best paper award partly for its pedagogical clarity. etcd, Consul, and CockroachDB chose Raft specifically because engineers could understand and debug it.

questions.question: What are the three states a Raft node can be in?

options.text: Active, Passive, Standby
Leader, Follower, Candidate
Primary, Secondary, Arbiter
Master, Replica, Observer

questions.explanation: Raft nodes transition between three states: Follower (passive, responds to leader/candidates), Candidate (during election, requests votes from peers), Leader (handles all client requests, replicates log entries). Only one leader exists per term. Most nodes spend most time as followers. The state machine is simple and well-defined, making Raft easier to implement correctly than Paxos.

questions.question: What is a 'term' in Raft?

options.text: A configuration parameter for election timeout duration
A logical time period; each term has at most one leader, terms increase monotonically
A network connection session between nodes
A database transaction boundary for log entries

questions.explanation: Terms are logical clocks in Raft. Each term starts with an election and has at most one leader. If a node sees a higher term in any message, it immediately updates its term and becomes a follower. Stale leaders are detected via term comparison—their requests are rejected. Terms provide a simple mechanism for distributed agreement on 'who's in charge now.'

questions.question: How does Raft leader election work?

options.text: Random selection weighted by node capacity
Follower times out, becomes candidate, requests votes; wins with majority
The node with the longest log automatically becomes leader
Administrator manually designates the leader node

questions.explanation: Election process: follower's election timeout expires → becomes candidate → increments term → votes for self → sends RequestVote RPCs to all other nodes. Wins with majority votes. Randomized timeouts (150-300ms typically) prevent split votes where multiple candidates tie. If no winner, timeout and try again with new term. Simple and deterministic.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the heartbeat in Raft?

options.text: To synchronize system clocks across all nodes
Leader sends periodic heartbeats to maintain authority and prevent new elections
To measure network latency between nodes
To trigger garbage collection of old log entries

questions.explanation: Leader sends empty AppendEntries RPCs (heartbeats) at regular intervals (typically 50-150ms). Followers reset their election timeout upon receiving a heartbeat. If no heartbeat arrives before timeout, a follower assumes the leader has failed and starts an election. Heartbeats are cheap (empty messages) but critical for cluster stability.

questions.question: How does Raft ensure log consistency across nodes?

options.text: Logs are stored in a centralized database accessible to all nodes
Leader's log is authoritative; followers must match leader's log to accept new entries
Each node maintains independent logs that are periodically reconciled
Logs are not used in Raft; it uses state snapshots instead

questions.explanation: Log Matching Property: if two logs have an entry with the same index and term, all preceding entries are identical. Leader includes prevLogIndex and prevLogTerm in AppendEntries; followers reject if there's a mismatch. This creates a consistency check chain back to the beginning. CockroachDB and TiKV rely on this property for their distributed SQL implementations.

questions.question: When is a log entry considered 'committed' in Raft?

options.text: When the leader writes it to its local log
When replicated to a majority of nodes and leader advances commit index
When all nodes in the cluster have acknowledged it
Immediately upon receiving the client request

questions.explanation: An entry is committed when stored on a majority of servers AND the leader has advanced its commitIndex past that entry. Committed entries are durable—guaranteed to eventually appear in all nodes' logs and safe to apply to the state machine. This majority requirement is why Raft tolerates (N-1)/2 failures. etcd won't acknowledge a write until it's committed.

questions.question: What happens if a Raft follower's log diverges from the leader's?

options.text: The follower becomes a candidate and triggers new election
Leader finds the latest matching entry and overwrites follower's conflicting entries
Both logs are merged using conflict resolution rules
The divergent follower is removed from the cluster

questions.explanation: Leader decrements nextIndex for that follower until finding a matching entry (same index and term). Then sends all entries from that point forward. Follower deletes any conflicting entries and appends the leader's entries. Leader's log always wins—this is safe because only committed entries matter, and the leader has all committed entries (election restriction ensures this).

questions.question: What is the 'election restriction' in Raft?

options.text: Only nodes with specific roles can participate in elections
A candidate must have a log at least as up-to-date as the voter's to receive their vote
Elections can only happen during specific time windows
A maximum of one election can occur per minute

questions.explanation: Voters deny their vote if the candidate's log is less up-to-date (compare last log term first, then log length). This ensures the elected leader has all committed entries—critical for safety. Without this restriction, a leader could be elected that's missing committed entries, violating durability guarantees. This is one of Raft's key safety mechanisms.

questions.question: Which systems use Raft for consensus? (Choose all that apply)

options.text: etcd
Consul
CockroachDB
TiKV

questions.explanation: Raft is widely adopted: etcd (Kubernetes' brain), Consul (HashiCorp service mesh), CockroachDB (distributed SQL), TiKV (TiDB's storage layer), RethinkDB, InfluxDB. Its understandability made it the go-to choice for new distributed systems. Engineers can actually debug Raft implementations, unlike Paxos where bugs are notoriously hard to find.

questions.question: How does Raft handle network partitions?

options.text: It pauses all operations until the partition heals
The partition with majority continues; minority partition can't elect leader or commit
Both partitions continue independently and merge later
The system automatically shuts down to prevent data corruption

questions.explanation: Majority partition: can elect leader, commit entries, serve clients normally. Minority partition: can't form quorum, no commits possible, may have candidates but they can't win elections. When the partition heals, minority nodes catch up from the majority's leader, potentially truncating any uncommitted entries. This is the CAP theorem in action—Raft chooses consistency over availability in minority partitions.

questions.question: What is a key difference between Raft and Paxos?

options.text: Raft is significantly slower than Paxos
Raft uses strong leader—all writes go through leader; Paxos allows any proposer
Paxos is easier to understand and implement
Raft doesn't provide consensus guarantees

questions.explanation: Raft uses a strong leader model: all client requests go through the leader, simplifying reasoning about the system. Paxos allows any node to propose values, which is more flexible but significantly more complex to implement correctly. Raft's leader-centric design was a deliberate choice to aid understandability. Both provide equivalent consensus guarantees; they differ in approach.
